text: Six children look over a wall at a beach.
From up here they see all of it at once. They cannot touch any of it.
Then they go down.
On the sand there is no view of the whole. There is a ball, cold water, and whatever happens next. Here they can change things.
Nobody on the sand knows how the day will end.
Donald Schön, who studied how professionals think, called this reflection-in-action: thinking while doing, from inside the thing you are changing.
Every step moves the sand, and the sand pushes back. Nobody down here can see the whole beach. Everybody down here can change it.
Later they climb back up. The beach is empty.
The day has not gone. It has gone behind them. Time moves forward, so what is done is at their backs, and they turn round to look at it.
The other half is often called reflection-on-action: thinking it over afterwards, from outside.
From up here the whole shape is there to see: every footprint, every turn. Reach down and push, and nothing moves.
So it is like this. In the moment, you can affect the world around you. Afterwards, you can only reflect back on it.
Reality is like that. Stand on a mountain and you can see the whole landscape. You cannot act inside it.
Memory is the same. So is time.
Walk out of your house and you can see its whole shape. You cannot move a chair.
Go back in and you can move the chair. You have lost the shape.
Nobody gets both at once.
A jigsaw puts it on a table. On the lid is the whole picture. In your hand is one piece.
Living is the pieces. Remembering is the lid.
The lid is not a photograph, though. Each time we remember, we make the picture again from a few bright pieces, and it comes out a little different.
Kierkegaard said it in two sentences. Life must be understood backwards. It must be lived forwards.
There is one thing wrong with the jigsaw. Its lid was printed before you opened the box.
Life is not like that. On the beach, every piece you lay changes the pieces that are left. Kick the ball and the game is a different game.
So picture a second jigsaw. The lid is blank. Each piece takes its colour from the pieces around it, and the lid is painted as you go.
We ran that puzzle a thousand times, from the same pieces. It finished as nine hundred and ninety-five different pictures.
Play it with someone else and the edge of each piece is cut by their last move. The picture is found, and it is made, and nobody made it alone.
Now step further back. A day is one piece. So is a year. So is a life.
From inside, a life feels like the next thing to do. From outside it has a shape, and people have always told that shape as a story.
Joseph Campbell called it the hero's journey: leave home, be tested, come back changed. Maureen Murdock answered with the heroine's journey, which is as much a return as a quest.
Ursula Le Guin went further. She said the first tool was probably not a spear. It was a bag: something to carry things home in, and to carry them to someone else.
The small self holds the piece. The large self is the picture. We are both, and we mostly forget the second.
Where do the big stories come from? Some have famous authors. The shapes inside them are older than any author.
Each teller kept what worked: whatever helped carry an experience from one person to the next. An archetype is the pattern that stayed, because it held. It is the lid, worn smooth by hands.
Edmund Burke called society a partnership between the living, the dead, and those who are to be born. Chesterton called tradition the democracy of the dead.
Science has a plainer word for it: a ratchet. Each generation starts where the last one stopped.
Look again at the wall the children are leaning on. Somebody built it, long before they were born.
Most of what holds us up was made by people we will never meet. We are doing the same, now, for people who will never meet us.
William Blake pictured that work as a city: ever building, ever falling.
To remember is, in a way, to re-member: to put the members back together. Nobody does that alone.
There is a trap in looking back. Suppose you only ever rehearsed the day you have.
You would score better and better on it, and worse on every new day. You would become very good at being who you were yesterday.
A measure that becomes the only target stops measuring. That is Goodhart's law.
Try to remember, not what happened when you were five, but how the world looked. You know it was different. You cannot say how. The ruler itself has changed.
There is a second trap, and this film is standing in it. We can become so interested in how the lid is made that we forget to play.
Nietzsche saw it in 1874. Too much looking back, he said, and a person can no longer act. To live at all, something has to be forgotten.
Our own time has made a habit of it: always one step outside, watching ourselves watch. Half of it is irony. Half of it badly wants to mean it.
Here is the joy of it. A great many people already know this. Love matters. Kindness matters. Nobody is doing it alone.
Still, we get stuck in our little loops. Our rules and our words can hold us too tightly, and the loudest maps can crowd out the land.
We have had enough of war. There is too much suffering.
Meanwhile the feeds are full of machines that will think for us: superintelligence, lore and prophecy, counted in views and likes.
The world feels very loud sometimes. Yes, this film too.
So something has to loosen the join. At night the clock stops mattering. The ball rolls uphill. The sea is in the wrong place. Nobody minds.
Everyone you meet in a dream is made by you. For a few hours you are the whole beach.
The dots are shaken and joined again. What comes out is not yesterday repeated. It is yesterday transformed.
One idea in science is that this is what dreams are for. They stop us fitting too closely to the days we have had. It is a hypothesis. The arithmetic behind it is sound.
Here is a child at the cinema. On the screen there is a storm at sea, and it is frightening.
So the child turns round and looks at the projector. A lamp, a strip of film, dust in the beam. It is only a picture. That helps.
Then the child turns back, because the story is better than the lamp.
Plato told a story like this nearly two and a half thousand years ago. Prisoners in a cave watch shadows on a wall. One of them turns round, sees the fire, and climbs out into the sun.
In another of his stories, souls drink from a river of forgetting before they are born.
Ram Dass put it more gently. He spoke of taking on the curriculum of being human. We forget, so that we can live the course we came for.
Looking at the projector is what this film has been doing. It works at the cinema, because the people on the screen cannot see you.
It does not work on the beach. On the beach the others can surprise you. They can tickle you, and you cannot tickle yourself. Your own touch is the one thing your brain always sees coming.
So a tickle is evidence. Someone is there who is not you. You are real because they are, and they are real because you are.
One more look at the projector, then. This voice is not a person. This film was put together with a machine that has read a great deal about beaches and has never been cold.
It is all lid. That is the joke: a film telling you to go and play, written with something that cannot go down to the sand.
Here is the surprising part. The film is not the machine's. A man with a photograph of six children kept saying no, not like that. Every scene changed because he was someone else.
That is the argument, happening. It took two.
In the morning you are somewhere again. Not everywhere, not nowhere, and not quite where you were.
The lid goes back on the shelf. The pieces are on the table, and one of them is in your hand.
That is what the beach is for. Go down again.
